title: What she holds
hookLine: a noose, a goad, a sugarcane bow and flower arrows, and what the hymn says they are
carry: desire and anger rest in her hands
tomorrow: a war told in names, and what she does after the battle
last: BORN FROM THE FIRE OF CONSCIOUSNESS.

lines: A ROPE, A HOOK, A BOW, ARROWS.
cards: A rope. A hook for steering an elephant. A bow cut from sugarcane.
Arrows tipped with flowers. That's what the goddess Lalita holds in her four hands, in paintings and temple images.

An odd inventory: a noose and a goad sound like tools for catching and driving animals, and a sugarcane bow sounds like something out of a children's story. But the Lalita Sahasranama doesn't leave the objects as objects.
A short run of names, early in the hymn, says what each one really is.

teach.b: After the names of her rising from a fire of consciousness, the hymn describes her form, and four names in a row say what she carries. In paraphrase: she holds the noose that is desire.
The Sanskrit there is raga: passion, attachment, the pull toward what we want.
She shines with the goad that is anger, the hooked stick that keeps an elephant moving or turns it aside. Her bow of sugarcane is the mind.

teach.h: THE BOW IS THE MIND, THE ARROWS THE SENSES.
teach.b: And her arrows are the five subtle elements, the tanmatras, the subtle forms of sound, touch, form, taste and smell, what the senses meet. Desire, anger, the mind, the senses.

The Bhagavad Gita traces how dwelling on things breeds attachment, attachment breeds desire, and desire breeds anger. These are the hard parts of an inner life, and in this hymn they aren't thrown away or trampled.
They're in the goddess's hands. Readers take that more than one way. Some say she holds them, so they have no hold on her.
Others hear something gentler: even a person's desire and anger are within her reach.
And notice the sweetness: the bow is sugarcane, the arrows are flowers, as in the old stories Kama, the god of love, carries; the path will come back to him tomorrow.

teach.h: WHAT A GOD HOLDS IS A LESSON.
teach.b: Here's the teaching, and you can see it on any shrine: in a Hindu image, what the god holds is a lesson. Lalita's hands say the hard parts of a person aren't outside the divine.
They're held, and steered, the way a goad steers an elephant instead of killing it.

how: Devotees of the goddess recite the Lalita Sahasranama at home or in temples, and images of Lalita show her four-armed, holding the noose, the goad, the sugarcane bow and the flower arrows the hymn describes.

o: a hymn of a thousand names for the goddess Lalita
a list of the weapons the gods gave to Lalita

games.q: the four hands: tap the pairs.
p: the subtle elements of the senses

s: in the hymn, Lalita throws desire and anger away
the names put them in her hands: the noose is desire, the goad is anger.
her bow is made of sugarcane
and a name in the hymn says the sugarcane bow is the mind.
her arrows stand for enemies she has beaten
the hymn names them the subtle elements: sound, touch, form, taste and smell.

games.q: you're painting Lalita for a home shrine, and the hymn tells you what goes in her hands. which list do you paint?
o: a sword, a shield, a spear and a trident.
a noose, a goad, a sugarcane bow and flower arrows.
a lotus, a book, a water pot and beads.
games.why: the hymn names a noose, a goad, a sugarcane bow and flower arrows, and then says what they are: desire, anger, the mind and the subtle elements of the senses.

practice: Bring to mind one small want you're carrying today and notice it the way you'd notice a rope in someone's hand: there, held; then one irritation, then the busy mind, then one sound or touch, each seen the same way. Nothing to fix.
If you pray, you can offer each to the goddess in your own words; if you don't, let them rest in open hands.

wordCard.voice: The Lalita Sahasranama. The hymn of names for the goddess Lalita, and today four of them: the noose, the goad, the bow and the arrows.

orig.note: Sanskrit pāśa: a noose, a rope for binding. in the hymn, Lalita's noose is desire (rāga).

carryVoice: Your line: desire and anger rest in her hands. Held, not thrown away. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.ref: Lalita Sahasranama, names 4 and 7–11 (Brahmanda Purana, Lalitopakhyana)
